title: Visions of God by the River Kebar
summary: In the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's exile, the priest Ezekiel, living among the exiles in Babylonia, sees the heavens open. Out of a storm cloud from the north come four living creatures with four faces and four wings, wheels full of eyes that move with them, and above them a crystal expanse supporting a throne. On the throne is a figure like a man, surrounded by brilliant light like a rainbow: the likeness of the glory of the LORD. Ezekiel falls on his face.
story: The book of Ezekiel opens with the exiles already in Babylon. In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar had taken King Jehoiachin and thousands of Judah's leading citizens away (2 Kings 24:10-16), and Ezekiel was among them. Jerusalem still stood, with Zedekiah on its throne, and many of the exiles expected to go home soon. Chapter 1 is the vision that begins Ezekiel's work as a prophet. Its message comes before any words are spoken: the God of Israel is not confined to the temple in Jerusalem. His throne moves. He can appear in the land of the Chaldeans, by a canal in a foreign country, to a priest who has lost his temple. The glory of the LORD seen here is the same glory Ezekiel will later watch depart from the defiled temple (chapters 10 and 11) and finally return to a new one (chapter 43).
historical:
The date is precise: the fifth day of the fourth month of the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile, which corresponds to the summer of 593 BC. Ezekiel counts years from Jehoiachin's deportation throughout the book, perhaps because many exiles still regarded Jehoiachin, not Zedekiah, as their rightful king. The thirtieth year of verse 1 is not explained. Many interpreters think it is Ezekiel's age, which would fit a priest reaching the age when priestly service began (Numbers 4:3); others have proposed that it counts from some other event, such as the discovery of the book of the law under Josiah, but there is no agreement.

The River Kebar was probably a canal rather than a natural river. Babylonian business documents from the city of Nippur, from the following century, mention a canal named Kabar in that area, and the exiles were settled in communities along the canal system of southern Mesopotamia. Ezekiel is identified as a priest, the son of Buzi (verse 3). As a priest from Jerusalem he would have been trained in the temple and its rituals, and the vision's imagery of cherubim, fire, and a throne is steeped in temple tradition.
cultural:
An ancient reader would recognize some of what Ezekiel saw. The temple in Jerusalem had cherubim, winged guardian figures, over the ark in the Most Holy Place and carved on its walls (1 Kings 6:23-29), and Israel spoke of the LORD as enthroned above the cherubim (1 Samuel 4:4). Later in the book Ezekiel identifies the living creatures as cherubim (10:20). Composite winged beings, combining human, lion, bull, and eagle features, also stood as guardians at the gates of Assyrian and Babylonian palaces and temples. Ezekiel's creatures belong to that visual world, but they guard no earthly palace; they bear the throne of the God of Israel.

Other details echo Israel's own traditions of God's appearing. Storm, cloud, fire, and brightness accompanied the LORD at Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:16-18). The throne above an expanse like crystal recalls the elders of Israel who saw under God's feet something like a pavement of sapphire, clear as the sky (Exodus 24:10). The sapphire of verse 26 was probably lapis lazuli, the deep blue stone prized across the ancient Near East. The rainbow of verse 28 recalls the sign of God's covenant after the flood (Genesis 9:13-16).
literary: The chapter is written as a first-person vision report, with a short third-person note (verses 2 and 3) that fixes the date and names the prophet. It moves from the edges inward and from the bottom upward: first the storm (verse 4), then the living creatures (verses 5 to 14), then the wheels beside them (verses 15 to 21), then the expanse above their heads (verses 22 to 25), then the throne and the figure seated on it (verses 26 to 28). Ezekiel's language is deliberately cautious. He repeatedly uses words like likeness, appearance, and like, piling them up as he approaches the throne until he speaks of the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD (verse 28). The effect is to show that he is describing something real while insisting that no human words can capture it. The vision is not a blueprint and cannot be drawn with precision; its details build an impression of holiness, power, and freedom of movement.

outline.t: The date and setting: a priest among the exiles
The storm and the four living creatures
The wheels that move with the creatures
The throne and the likeness of the glory of the LORD

doctrines.note: The vision shows God as sovereign and free. His throne is not fixed in Jerusalem; it can move in any direction without turning (verse 17). The exiles had not left God behind when they left the land.

Everything in the vision is fire, brightness, and awe, and Ezekiel's response is to fall on his face (verse 28). The chapter shows the holiness of God as overwhelming, not as an idea but as a presence before which a human being cannot stand unaided.

“The heavens opened and I saw visions of God” (verse 1). God makes himself known on his own initiative, and even then only in likenesses. The chapter models both the reality of revelation and its limits: God is truly seen, but not fully comprehended.

words.note: Kavod, glory. The root means weight or heaviness, and it came to mean honor, importance, and splendor. In the priestly tradition the glory of the LORD is the visible radiance of his presence, which filled the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11). Its appearance in Babylon is the chapter's great surprise.

Chayyah, a living thing or living creature. It usually refers to animals, but here it names the four heavenly beings who carry the throne. They are later identified as cherubim (10:20). Revelation 4 describes four living creatures around God's throne with the faces of a lion, an ox, a man, and an eagle.

Demut, likeness or resemblance. The same word appears in Genesis 1:26, where humanity is made in God's likeness. Ezekiel uses it ten times in this chapter to mark the distance between what he saw and the reality: he saw the likeness of a throne and a figure like a man, not God as he is in himself.

Ophan, wheel. The wheels full of eyes that move with the creatures suggest a throne that is mobile and all-seeing. Later Jewish tradition called Ezekiel's vision the merkavah, the chariot, and treated its study with special care.

christ: The vision ends with the likeness of a figure like that of a man on the throne of God (verse 26). Ezekiel does not explain this, and it is not a hidden prediction. But the New Testament shows where it leads. John writes that no one has ever seen God, but the only Son has made him known (John 1:18), and that in Jesus the glory of God was seen dwelling among us (John 1:14). Paul speaks of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). In Revelation 1, John sees the risen Christ with features drawn from Ezekiel's vision (a voice like many waters, brightness like fire and bronze) and falls at his feet as Ezekiel did. For Christians the human figure on the throne anticipates the incarnate Son, fully God and fully man, who now reigns at the Father's right hand. The early church writer Irenaeus also linked the four faces to the four Gospels, a traditional reading that is devotional rather than exegetical.

hard.q: What exactly did Ezekiel see, and how should a modern reader picture it?
hard.a: Ezekiel himself refuses to give a precise picture. His words for what he saw are hedged at every point: the form of, the appearance of, like, the likeness of. He is describing a vision, not a physical object observed under ordinary conditions, and the chapter's own framing is that he saw visions of God (verse 1). Attempts to draw the scene as a diagram or reconstruct it as a machine break down quickly, because they ignore both the text's genre and its explicit identification of the scene as the glory of the LORD. Jewish tradition was cautious in another way, restricting public teaching of this chapter for fear of speculation. The best approach is to read it as Ezekiel intends: as a set of images drawn from temple, storm, and throne, meant to convey God's majesty, freedom, and presence among the exiles. What the reader is meant to take away is not a sketch but the prophet's response: awe, humility, and readiness to listen.

questions: The exiles thought they had left God behind in Jerusalem. Where have you felt far from God, and what does this vision say about his presence there?
Ezekiel keeps saying likeness and appearance. Why do you think he is so careful not to claim he has described God exactly?
The vision leaves Ezekiel on his face. When was the last time a sense of God's greatness humbled you, and how did it change you?
